ety.text: First attested in mid 13th century. From Middle English abrood (“broadly widely scattered”), from a- (“on, in”) + brood (“broad”). Equivalent to a- + broad.

senses.d: Beyond the bounds of a country; in foreign countries.
ex: Another prince, deposed by the Revolution, was living abroad.

senses.d: At large; widely; broadly; over a wide space.
ex: A tree spreads its branches abroad.
"Faither!" I cried as I undid the bolt and pushed the leaves of the door abroad, "Faither, ye are welcome hame!"

senses.d: Without a certain confine; outside the house; away from one's abode.
ex: I went to St. James', where another was preaching in the court abroad.
Again: The lonely fox roams far abroad, / On ſecret rapine bent and midnight fraud; […]

senses.d: Before the public at large; throughout society or the world; here and there; moving without restriction.
ex: This Peece, or Schisme of Suicisme, and Selfishnesse, hath spawned most of the Heresies and Schismes, that are abroad in the World.

senses.d: Not on target; astray; in error; confused; dazed.
Played elsewhere than one's home grounds.

ex: That is not a xenophobic remark. I am a xenophiliac; I love abroad. I love foreigners. I just do not like the way that they are running the European agricultural policy.
[...] as her father had an abroad trip, he had dropped her mother here.
He had contracted the disease during an abroad trip to draw up an agreement for the mass production of low-power engines.
